plan_a_advantages: Specifically targets climbing strength and trail-specific power with dedicated hill workouts.
Includes more frequent shorter sessions, potentially aiding recovery and preventing burnout.
Prioritizes building a foundation of aerobic consistency alongside strength work.
plan_b_advantages: Incorporates more tempo and interval work, which can improve speed and efficiency.
Features longer runs, which are important for overall endurance, though not as directly targeted for trail speed as Plan A’s hill work.
reasoning: Plan A is the better training plan for a trail runner aiming to become faster, primarily because it directly addresses the key demands of trail running – climbing strength and trail-specific power – through a significant focus on hill workouts. Plan B, while including some tempo and interval work, prioritizes aerobic endurance and doesn't dedicate enough volume to the specific adaptations needed for trail speed. Plan A’s consistent hill sessions will build the muscular endurance crucial for sustained uphill efforts, a hallmark of trail racing, while Plan B’s longer, steady runs might not translate to the same level of power and efficiency on technical terrain. Furthermore, the inclusion of shorter, more frequent ‘easy’ runs in Plan A aids in recovery and prevents overtraining, which is vital for consistent progress.
